one_paragraph_summary: The Supreme Court issued the writ of amparo in Deduro v. Vinoya (July 4, 2023, released only May 8, 2024) to protect petitioner Siegfred Deduro after he was Red-tagged by the government. Panganiban hails the unanimous 39-page ponencia of Justice Rodil V. Zalameda as a 'well-written treatise' on the writ's (1) purpose, (2) coverage, (3) parties, and (4) process. He recalls retired Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna's 1991 bar question on the writ -- very few examinees answered correctly -- and his personal interview with Azcuna, who traces the writ's origins to Mexico and Prof. Héctor Fix-Zamudio. As a delegate to the 1971 Constitutional Convention Azcuna proposed its inclusion 'but failed because only a few understood it then'; as a member of the 1986 Constitutional Commission he tried again to place it in the Bill of Rights, but the late CJ Roberto Concepcion convinced him to incorporate it under SC powers, where it now lives. For his 'untiring spade work,' CJ bestows on him the title 'Father of the Writ of Amparo in the Philippines.' He then distinguishes the writ of amparo from the privilege of the writ: the writ is issued when, 'on its face,' the petition and affidavits show prima facie violation of the right to life, liberty, or security; the privilege follows only after 'summary proceedings' requiring 'substantial evidence' -- analogous (but not identical) to a preliminary vs permanent injunction in civil cases (with proof scales of prima facie, substantial, preponderance, and beyond reasonable doubt). So Deduro's writ is 'a good start' but to complete his victory he must produce substantial evidence to earn the privilege. Coverage extends to extralegal killings (per UN instruments, killings without due process regardless of motive, by state or non-state actors), enforced disappearances (per RA 10353), and threats thereof -- and SND v. Manalo (Oct. 7, 2008) recognizes the right to security as 'freedom from fear,' independent of any liberty deprivation. Red-tagging as a 'communist' or 'terrorist' is actionable harassment because it exposes the target to vigilantes, paramilitary groups, or state agents -- and creates justifiable fear of killing or abduction. For lack of space, CJ leaves parties and process to lawyers and law students reading the Zalameda treatise -- which 'could erupt in another bar exam.'
